title: The Wardrobe of Milton Flats
premise: Wendell Eastwick has spent eleven years writing postcards to his mother at Milton Flats, the tenement that burned the night she died, mailing them to an address that no longer exists. At his father's funeral, a woman named Ida Corrigan calls the family by their true surname — Eastwick-Byrne — and reveals she was the lodger who survived the fire, the one Wendell's mother went back inside to save, and the reason his father never spoke of that night again. As Wendell and Ida excavate the family's buried history through letters, photographs, and the salvaged wardrobe his mother hid things in, Wendell must decide whether the man in the old photographs — his father, young and complicit in a terrible choice — deserves forgiveness before Ida's illness takes her, and before he loses the chance to say what the postcards never could.
about_author: Odile Ashgrove is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed letters in a northern postal dead-letter office. She writes about families who communicate best through objects, and lives above a shuttered tailor's shop with a wardrobe she refuses to open.

chapters.title: Poste Restante
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He mails his 4,000th postcard to the burned ruin of Milton Flats, then learns his estranged father has died. The chapter establishes his ritual of unsent truths and his numb, ordered life. Emotional beat: grief deferred so long it has become furniture.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Grey Coat
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. At the funeral, a stranger weeps harder than anyone and calls the family 'the Byrnes.' Wendell confronts her; she says only, 'Ask him about the wardrobe,' and leaves a key in his palm. Beat: the first crack in Wendell's careful inventory of silence.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Sorting his father's flat, he finds the wardrobe from Milton Flats, scorched at one corner, locked. Inside: his mother's letters, addressed to Ida Corrigan, never sent. Beat: vertigo — his private ritual mirrored by his mother's.

chapters.title: Ida
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. In her hospital room, Ida reads her own decades-old diary and recalls the fire only in fragments: a hand on her wrist, smoke, a name shouted down a stairwell. She is dying and has come back to finish something. Beat: dread braided with tenderness.

chapters.title: What the Fire Kept
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He tracks Ida down and demands answers. She tells him she was the lodger his mother died saving — and that his father barred the door behind her. Wendell refuses to believe it. Beat: the ground tilts; loyalty becomes a question.

chapters.title: The Photographs
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Among his father's effects, photographs show his parents young with Ida between them, laughing — and one negative of his father at the flats' door on the night of the fire, watching. Beat: the stranger in the pictures is his own father, and Wendell cannot look away.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Alternating Wendell/Ida POV. They read the mother's letters aloud together; she wrote to Ida for years after the fire, begging forgiveness for a debt neither will name. Beat: two strangers become co-conspirators in a dead woman's voice.

chapters.title: Milton Flats, Rebuilt in Memory
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. Ida walks Wendell through the building as it was, room by room, reconstructing the night: the landlord's illegal partitions, the blocked exit, the choice his father made to save himself and let his wife go back in. Beat: horror arriving gently, which makes it worse.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He rages — at Ida for surviving, at his father for choosing, at his mother for going back. He burns a letter and instantly regrets it. Beat: anger as the last defense against grief.

chapters.title: A Debt in Winter
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. Flashback chapters begin: 1978, Ida newly arrived, pregnant, hiding from someone; the Eastwick-Byrnes take her in against the landlord's rules. Beat: warmth with a fault line running under it.

chapters.title: The Second Key
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A locksmith opens the wardrobe's hidden drawer: inside, his mother's savings book and a deed — she had secretly bought the plot where Milton Flats stood, intending to rebuild it as rooms for people like Ida. Beat: the mother Wendell knew was a stranger too, a better one.

chapters.title: What My Father Carried
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. Flashback: the father knew about the pregnancy, the danger, the money; his silence after the fire was not cowardice alone but a bargain he made with the landlord to keep Ida out of court. Beat: moral complexity — survival purchased with complicity.

chapters.title: The Man Who Stayed Silent
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. He finds his father's own unsent letters — forty of them, all to Ida, all beginning 'I do not ask you to forgive me.' Beat: Wendell recognizes his postcards; the inheritance of unsayable things is literal.

chapters.title: Hospital Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. Ida's condition worsens; she asks Wendell to read her the mother's final letter, which she has never dared open. They agree to open it together. Beat: intimacy forged by shared dread.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Shared POV. The mother's letter forgives them both — husband and lodger — but asks one thing: that the land be used, that the rebuilding happen, that no one keep her in a wardrobe. Beat: catharsis and a task; grief acquires a direction.

chapters.title: Objections
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Relatives contest the deed; the family wants the land sold. Wendell, for the first time in his life, publicly claims the name Eastwick-Byrne and fights. Beat: love against duty — duty says sell, love says build.

chapters.title: Ashgrove
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. Ida confesses her final secret: the person she was hiding from in 1978 was the child's father, and the child — given up — grew up to be the lawyer opposing them. Beat: the past arrives wearing a suit and holding paperwork.

chapters.title: The Meeting
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell meets Ida's son privately and shows him the photographs, the letters, the wardrobe. The son withdraws the objection — not from mercy, but because he recognizes the ritual of unsaid things as his own inheritance too. Beat: forgiveness begins as recognition.

chapters.title: Breaking Ground
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. On the burned plot, they break ground on the house his mother planned; Ida, in a wheelchair, lays the first stone from the original chimney. Beat: quiet triumph, shadowed by time running out.

chapters.title: The Wardrobe Opens
chapters.summary: Ida's POV. Ida asks to see the wardrobe one last time; Wendell carries her to it and they empty it together, item by item, reading everything aloud until nothing unsaid remains inside it. Beat: the inventory finally complete.

chapters.title: What Time Was Running Out Of
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Ida dies at dawn in the new house's unfinished first room. Wendell writes his last postcard — to her — and mails it to the address that now exists. Beat: grief transfigured into address; the circle closed.

chapters.title: Eastwick-Byrne
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, epilogue. A year later, the house is full of tenants like the woman Ida once was; Wendell keeps the wardrobe, empty, its scorched corner facing the light. He signs his name fully for the first time. Beat: inheritance accepted — the price paid forward, not repeated.
